extracted.intended_audience: organizations preparing sustainability reports (report preparers, sustainability officers, reporting teams) using the GRI Standards
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements and guidance for preparing sustainability reports in accordance with the GRI Sustainability Reporting Standards, including how to determine material topics, disclose information, use Sector and Topic Standards, and publish a GRI content index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 1: Apply the reporting principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall apply all the reporting principles specified in section 4 of GRI 1: Foundation 2021.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting principles are fundamental to ensuring the quality of the reported information. They must be applied by the organization when preparing reported information (see section 4 for the principles and further explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 2: Report the disclosures in GRI 2: General Disclosures 2021
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall report all disclosures in GRI 2: General Disclosures 2021.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes Disclosure 2-1 Organizational details; 2-2 Entities included in the organization’s sustainability reporting; 2-3 Reporting period, frequency and contact point; 2-4 Restatements of information; 2-5 External assurance, etc. Reasons for omission are permitted for all disclosures in GRI 2 except for specified exceptions (the Standard indicates which disclosures cannot be omitted). If the organization cannot comply with a disclosure (where omission is permitted), it must specify the disclosure and provide a reason for omission with explanation in the GRI content index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 3: Determine material topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall determine its material topics based on its specific circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process must be informed by ongoing identification and assessment of impacts and by stakeholder engagement and expert input. The organization must review applicable Sector Standards (if available) to determine whether each topic listed is material; if a Sector Standard topic is determined not material, the organization must list it in the GRI content index and explain why. See GRI 3: Material Topics for step-by-step guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 4: Report the disclosures in GRI 3: Material Topics 2021
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall report its process of determining material topics and how it manages each material topic using the disclosures in GRI 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Disclosure 3-1 to report the process, Disclosure 3-2 to report the list of material topics, and Disclosure 3-3 to report management of material topics. Reasons for omission are only permitted for Disclosure 3-3; if the organization cannot comply with 3-3 (or requirements within it) it must specify this in the GRI content index and provide a reason for omission with explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 5: Report disclosures from the GRI Topic Standards for each material topic
rubrics_metrics.description: For each material topic, the organization shall report relevant disclosures from the GRI Topic Standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization must identify disclosures from Topic Standards that are relevant to its impacts for each material topic and report only those relevant disclosures. There is no minimum number of disclosures—reporting depends on relevance. If Topic Standard disclosures do not provide sufficient information, the organization should report additional disclosures (e.g., sector recommended disclosures, disclosures from other sources, or organization-developed disclosures) that match the rigor of the GRI Standards. Reasons for omission are permitted for all Topic Standard disclosures; if the organization cannot comply it must state the disclosure and provide a reason in the content index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 6: Provide reasons for omission
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall provide reasons for omission for disclosures and requirements it cannot comply with where reasons for omission are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclosure or a requirement within a disclosure cannot be complied with (e.g., due to confidentiality or legal prohibitions), the organization must specify the disclosure/requirement and give a reason for omission with explanation in the GRI content index. The Standard specifies which disclosures do not permit omission (e.g., certain items in GRI 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 7: Publish a GRI content index
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall publish a GRI content index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GRI content index provides an overview of reported information, shows where information users can find it (locations or links), and demonstrates which GRI Standards and disclosures the organization has used. If information is published across multiple locations (webpages, annual reports), the content index can point to those locations rather than repeating content. The index must also list Sector Standard topics determined as not material (if applicable) and explain why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 8: Provide a statement of use
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall provide a statement of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement of use indicates which GRI Standards have been used by the organization when preparing its reported information (e.g., which Universal, Sector, and Topic Standards were applied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement 9: Notify GRI
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization shall notify GRI when preparing reports in accordance with the GRI Standards (as required by the Standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification requirement is part of the 'in accordance' rules; the Standard requires organizations to notify GRI (procedural detail in the Standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: System of GRI Standards: Use of Universal, Sector and Topic Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The GRI Standards are a system of interrelated standards organized into Universal Standards (GRI 1, GRI 2, GRI 3), Sector Standards, and Topic Standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All organizations must apply the Universal Standards. Organizations use Sector Standards relevant to sectors they operate in when determining material topics and identifying likely disclosures. Organizations select Topic Standards according to their list of material topics. Figure 1 indicates: apply all Universal Standards; use Sector Standards that apply; select Topic Standards for reporting on material topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sector Standards to identify likely material topics and disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicable Sector Standards exist, the organization shall review each topic described in those Sector Standards and determine whether it is material, and use the Sector Standards to identify Topic Standard disclosures to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a topic in an applicable Sector Standard is determined not material, the organization must list it in the content index and explain why. For material topics covered by a Sector Standard, the Sector Standard may list Topic Standard disclosures recommended for reporting; the organization should report those disclosures or provide the required 'not applicable' reason for omission and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting principles and their role in quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting principles specified in section 4 (e.g., principles relating to completeness, accuracy, balance, clarity, comparability, timeliness, reliability — see Standard) underpin the quality of reported information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization is required to apply these principles; they guide how to prepare and present disclosures so that information users can make informed assessments. (The Standard presents the principles and elaborates what each entails and how to apply them.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting format and referencing (multilocation reporting and content index linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization can publish reported information in multiple formats and locations (standalone report, web pages, annual report); the content index should indicate where each disclosure is located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing a standalone report, organizations do not need to repeat information already published elsewhere; they can reference the location in the content index (e.g., links, page citations). 'Reported information' and 'report' refer to information across all locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: All GRI Standards have an effective date; the organization must use the Standard for information published on or after that effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: GRI 1: Foundation 2021 effective date is 1 January 2023 — information published on or after that date must use GRI 1. Effective dates consider adoption time; adoption before effective date is encouraged as best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements, guidance and defined terms conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the GRI Standards, requirements are presented in bold and indicated by the word 'shall'; guidance includes background, explanations and examples and is not mandatory; 'should' indicates a recommendation and 'can' indicates an option. Defined terms are underlined and linked to Glossary definitions which are required to be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations must comply with 'shall' requirements to report in accordance with the Standards. Guidance and recommendations help interpretation but are not mandatory. The Glossary terms have prescribed meanings and must be applied where used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key concept — Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact: the effect an organization has or could have on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights) as a result of its activities or business relationships. Impacts can be actual or potential, negative or positive, short- or long-term, intended or unintended, reversible or irreversible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impacts indicate the organization’s contribution (negative or positive) to sustainable development. Examples: economic impacts (taxes, procurement), environmental impacts (energy use, emissions), impacts on people (employment practices, supply chain working conditions). Impacts are interrelated across the three dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key concept — Material topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Material topics are those topics that represent an organization’s most significant impacts on the economy, environment, and people (including human rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations may identify many impacts but must prioritize reporting on most significant impacts. Topics group related impacts (e.g., 'water and effluents') to report cohesively. Determination of material topics is informed by ongoing impact identification and assessment, stakeholder engagement, and use of Sector Standards. Material topics cannot be deprioritized because they are not financially material; sustainability reporting is independent of financial materiality judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key concept — Due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Due diligence: the process through which an organization identifies, prevents, mitigates, and accounts for how it addresses its actual and potential negative impacts on the economy, environment, and people, including human rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations should avoid causing or contributing to negative impacts and address such impacts (including remediation where caused or contributed). For negative impacts directly linked by business relationships, organizations should seek to prevent or mitigate them even if they did not contribute; they are not automatically responsible for remediation but may play a role. If not feasible to address all impacts at once, prioritize based on severity and likelihood; for potential negative human rights impacts, severity takes precedence over likelihood. Due diligence aligns with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and OECD guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key concept — Stakeholder identification and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders are individuals or groups with interests that are affected or could be affected by the organization’s activities; stakeholder engagement helps identify and manage impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common stakeholder categories include employees, suppliers, communities, investors, customers, governments, NGOs, vulnerable groups. Organizations should identify relevant stakeholders for specific activities, engage directly where possible or via credible representatives/proxies, and consult experts where needed. Distinguish between affected and potentially affected stakeholders (important for remediation), and consider stakeholders unable to articulate views (e.g., future generations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and supplementing Topic Standard disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting Topic Standard disclosures, organizations report only disclosures relevant to their impacts; if Topic Standards do not fully cover a material topic, organizations should report additional disclosures from Sector recommendations, other sources, or organization-developed metrics of equivalent rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement for a minimum set of Topic disclosures; selection is driven by relevance to impacts. Organization-developed or externally sourced disclosures should align with authoritative instruments and have the same rigor as GRI disclosures. Example provided: pay equality may draw disclosures from multiple Topic Standards (e.g., GRI 202 and GRI 405).
